concept.name: Interest rate parity
concept.definition: The family of equilibrium conditions linking spot and forward exchange rates to interest rate differentials between two currencies. It comprises covered interest parity — a no-arbitrage condition tying the forward premium to the interest differential — and uncovered interest parity, which relates the interest differential to the expected change in the spot rate.
concept.intuition: Money should earn the same total return wherever it is parked once currency effects are accounted for; IRP is the statement of that idea, hedged (covered) or unhedged (uncovered).
concept.mechanics: In its covered form, borrowing in one currency, converting at spot, investing in the other, and locking in the conversion back with a forward must yield no riskless profit, forcing F/S to equal the ratio of gross interest returns. The uncovered form replaces the forward rate with the expected future spot rate and is a hypothesis about expectations rather than a pure arbitrage condition. Spot/forward pricing of FX swaps is read off these parity relations.
concept.formula: Covered: F/S = (1 + r_q x T)/(1 + r_b x T). Uncovered: E[S_T]/S = (1 + r_q x T)/(1 + r_b x T), with S and F in quote currency per base currency, r_q and r_b the two interest rates, T the tenor.
concept.failure_modes: CIP has been systematically violated since 2008 (persistent cross-currency basis) because of hedging demand and limits to arbitrage from bank balance-sheet constraints. UIP fails empirically as well: high-interest-rate currencies tend to appreciate rather than depreciate, the 'forward premium puzzle'.
concept.misconceptions: IRP is not a law that markets obey at all times; only the covered version is arbitrage-enforced, and even it has broken down persistently since the financial crisis.
concept.example: If 1-year rates are 5% in USD and 1% in JPY, CIP requires the 1-year USD/JPY forward to trade roughly 4% below spot; a materially different forward would open a covered arbitrage.

citations.source: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (Borio, McCauley, McGuire, Sushko)
